propositions.text: The claimant and her son are Chinese citizens fearing persecution for religion and social group membership under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The claimant claims to have well-founded fear of persecution at the hands of the Communist regime and in particular, the Public Security Bureau, by reason of her religion as a Christian and her son as a member of a particular social group under sections 96 and 97 of The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant and her son are Chinese citizens fearing persecution for religion and social group membership under IRPA sections 96 and 97, says the court.

propositions.text: The claimant was appointed designated representative of her minor son.
propositions.quote: The claimant was appointed the designated representative of her son, a minor.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant was appointed designated representative of her minor son, says the court.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges she joined an underground Christian church after divorce and it was raided by PSB in 2012, leading to her escape and flight to Canada.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges in her Personal Information Form that as a result of going through a divorce, she turned to an underground Christian church on the recommendation of a friend. The claimant maintains that she started to attend the underground Christian church in XXXX 2011. The claimant indicated that on XXXX XXXX, 2012, her underground Christian church was raided by the Public Security Bureau (the PSB). The claimant indicated that she was able to escape and went to the home of a relative. The claimant alleges that the PSB went to her home to arrest her for her underground Christian church activities. The claimant stated that arrangements were made with a snakehead (smuggler) to leave the country. The claimant came to Canada on or about February 11, 2012, and claimed for refugee protection a few days later.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges she joined an underground Christian church after divorce and it was raided by PSB in 2012, leading to her escape and flight to Canada.

propositions.text: The claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection; they failed to prove serious persecution or risk of torture or cruel treatment if returned to China.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. I find that the claimants have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that on the balance of probabilities they would personally be subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to the People's Republic of China.

paragraphs.summary: The claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection; they failed to prove serious persecution or risk of torture or cruel treatment if returned to China, finds the court.

propositions.text: The claimant's oral testimony and documents establish their identities as Chinese citizens and claimant as member of underground church in China.
propositions.quote: The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documents filed establish their identities as citizens of the People's Republic of China. The claimant as a Member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's testimony and documents establish their Chinese citizenship and claimant's membership in an underground church, says the court.

propositions.text: The claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in China due to limited differences in religious practice and implausible PSB raid story.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in the People's Republic of China. ... I reject this explanation. ... In summary, I find that the claimant was never a member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China, due to her extremely limited differences in practising her religion in the People's Republic of China and here in Canada as well as the implausible and not credible of the PSB running in the front door so she could run out the back door.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant was never a member of an underground Christian church in China due to limited religious practice differences and implausible PSB raid story.

propositions.text: The summons from PSB is not an arrest summons and is not authentic; letter from friend about raid is not credible.
propositions.quote: The summons does not indicate that it is an "Arrest Summons" and that it is simply for the claimant to appear. ... I therefore do not find that the summons proffered by the claimant to be authentic. ... I do not give this document any weight as the author was not present to determine the veracity of it and also I have found that the claimant was not a member of an underground church in the People's Republic of China.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the PSB summons is not an arrest summons and not authentic; letter about raid is not credible.

propositions.text: The claimant is a Christian in Canada, supported by baptism certificates and church letter.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is a Christian in Canada. ... the claimant filed Certificates of Baptism for herself and the minor claimant, as well as a church letter dated January 5, 2018, attesting to her membership in that church from February 26, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant is a Christian in Canada, supported by baptism certificates and church letter.

propositions.text: Whether claimant faces serious possibility of persecution if returning to China and joining underground Christian church.
propositions.quote: I must determine, whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if she returns to the People's Republic of China and chooses to become a member of an underground Christian church.

paragraphs.summary: The court must determine if claimant faces serious persecution risk if returning to China and joining underground church.

propositions.text: Fujian province has most liberal religious policy in China; few documented incidents of persecution there.
propositions.quote: I note the documentary evidence suggests by virtue of the absence of evidence of incidents of persecution in Fujian has the most liberal policy on religion in the People's Republic of China. ... found only four incidents in Fujian: one, involving a church built in Fuqing that was forcibly demolished. ... The second incident was in 2006 that there was a demolition of a house church somewhere in Fujian ... and the last in October 2010 that a worker was taken away and sealed three venues used for church gatherings of a church in Lianjiang County in Fujian ...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Fujian province has the most liberal religious policy in China with few documented persecution incidents.

propositions.text: Reports indicate Fujian is relatively liberal with a thriving Christian community and local government tolerance of unregistered believers.
propositions.quote: The report of Professor T. Lambert indicates that the religious policy in Fujian as relatively liberal and that it has a thriving and rapidly growing Christian community. ... local government in Fujian seems fairly tolerant of unregistered believers as it is rare that one reads of cases of persecution of house church Christians in this province.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reports indicate Fujian is relatively liberal with a thriving Christian community and local government tolerance.

propositions.text: If arrests of Christians occurred in Fujian in 2012 or later, there would be documentation; none found.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were arrests of Christians in Fujian in 2012 or thereafter, there would be some documentation of these arrests.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds if Christian arrests occurred in Fujian in 2012 or later, there would be documentation; none found.

propositions.text: Maldonado principle creates presumption that claimant's sworn allegations are true unless reasons to doubt.
propositions.quote: The principle in Maldonado is that when a refugee claimant swears to tell the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness.

paragraphs.summary: The Maldonado principle presumes claimant's sworn allegations true unless reasons to doubt, explains prior court.

propositions.text: Presumption of truthfulness is rebuttable by documentary evidence failing to mention expected facts.
propositions.quote: However, the presumption that a claimant's own testimony is true is always rebuttable and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect to mention.

paragraphs.summary: The presumption of truthfulness is rebuttable by documentary evidence failing to mention expected facts, explains prior court.

propositions.text: If underground Christians faced serious persecution in Fujian, it would have been documented, supported by Federal Court decision.
propositions.quote: I am supported in this analysis by the Federal Court decision by Justice Crampton who found that it was reasonable for the Board to find that, if underground Christians faced a serious possibility of persecution in Fujian Province, it would have been documented.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds, supported by Federal Court, that serious persecution of underground Christians in Fujian would have been documented.

propositions.text: Risk of persecution requires considering laws and their application; existence of harsh laws alone insufficient.
propositions.quote: I recognize that even if the evidence speaks of some harm that would qualify as serious, I must consider whether there is a serious possibility that the harm will actually come to pass. ... The Supreme Court has emphasized that, in a determination as to whether the claimant's fear is objectively well founded, the relevant factors include the laws in the claimant's homeland, together with the manner in which they are applied.

paragraphs.summary: The court states risk of persecution requires considering laws and their application; harsh laws alone insufficient, citing Supreme Court.

propositions.text: Claimant and son are free to worship in any church in Fujian; documentary evidence is reliable and probative.
propositions.quote: This leads me to determine that the claimant (and the minor claimant) are free to choose to worship in the Christian congregation of her choosing. I have chosen to rely on the documentary evidence because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably be expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation of Christians in Fujian.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant and son free to worship in any church in Fujian, relying on reliable documentary evidence.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, claimant and son can practice religion freely in Fujian without serious persecution risk.
propositions.quote: I have considered the documentary evidence and I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant (and the minor claimant) would be able to practice their religion in any church in Fujian Province if they were to return to the their home in Fujian province in the People's Republic of China and that there is not a serious possibility that they would be persecuted for doing so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds on balance of probabilities claimant and son can practice religion freely in Fujian without serious persecution risk.

propositions.text: Decision supported by Federal Court decisions noting documentation of persecution in Fujian would exist if it occurred.
propositions.quote: I am supported in this decision by a decision of Mr. Justice Russell. In reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin concerning Fujian Province ... it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian Province it would have been documented. ... Justice Lemieux in Jiang noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian Province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice and people generally practice their religion freely.

paragraphs.summary: The court's decision is supported by Federal Court decisions noting persecution in Fujian would be documented if it occurred.

propositions.text: Federal Court has held Board's finding that Christians may practice freely in Fujian is reasonable.
propositions.quote: In another Federal Court decision in the case of Yao Justice O'Keefe notes that "this Court has held on several occasions that the Board's finding that Christians may practice freely in Fujian Province is reasonable".

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court has held Board's finding that Christians may practice freely in Fujian is reasonable, explains prior court.

propositions.text: The claimant fears arrest by the PSB for underground church activities if returned to China.
propositions.quote: The claimant, when asked by the panel, as to what she fears if she were to return to the People's Republic of China, indicated that she would be arrested by the PSB for activities at her underground church.

propositions.text: The claimant only mentioned fear of forced IUD after counsel's prompting due to nervousness.
propositions.quote: It was not until her counsel prompted her as to what else she fears if she returns to her home country that she mentioned that she does not want to be forced to wear an IUD, as she now has two children

propositions.text: The claimant's explanation of nervousness for not mentioning forced IUD fear is rejected.
propositions.quote: When asked by the panel why she did not indicate her fear of being forced to wear an IUD, the claimant replied that she was too nervous. I reject this explanation

propositions.text: Fear of forced birth control is a major part of the claimant's claim.
propositions.quote: as the fear of forced type of birth control is a major part of her claim.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant fears PSB arrest and forced IUD; rejects her nervousness explanation for late mention of IUD fear.

propositions.text: The claimant has two children: one born in Canada, one in China.
propositions.quote: The claimant has two children as previously indicated, one born in Canada and one born in the People's Republic of China.

propositions.text: The Canadian-born child would not count towards family planning child limits in China.
propositions.quote: I find that the child born in Canada would not be considered in determining the number of children for family planning purposes in the People's Republic of China.

propositions.text: Article 10 of Fujian Province Regulations excludes overseas-born children from family planning counts.
propositions.quote: Article 10 of the Regulations of Fujian Province on Population and Family Planning28states: When both the husband and wife are Chinese returned from overseas, whose children were born overseas and are residents of foreign countries before they returned to China for settlement, the number of such children of theirs shall not be counted towards the number of children in this Regulation on Population and Family Planning.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the Canadian-born child is excluded from China's family planning child count per Fujian regulations.

propositions.text: The claimant is single and her Canadian-born child is out of wedlock.
propositions.quote: Although the claimant is single and her Canadian-born child born out of wedlock

propositions.text: Country documents say children born out of wedlock have equal rights to those born in wedlock.
propositions.quote: country documentation29 indicates that children who are born out of wedlock should not be discriminated against and shall enjoy the same rights as children born in wedlock.

propositions.text: The claimant would not be forced to wear an IUD because her Canadian-born child is not counted under China's two-child policy.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I find that the claimant would not be forced to wear an IUD upon returning to the People's Republic of China as her Canadian-born child would not be counted towards the two-child family planning policy in the People's Republic of China.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant's single status and child's out-of-wedlock birth do not affect her not being forced to wear an IUD.

propositions.text: If the Canadian-born child counted, the claimant still would not be forced to wear an IUD under Fujian regulations.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, if the Canadian-born child of the claimant is counted towards the two-child family planning in the People's Republic of China, she would not be forced to wear an IUD, as Article 16 of the Regulations of Fujian Province on Population and Family Planning30 states

propositions.text: Article 16 allows couples with children to choose their own contraceptive methods.
propositions.quote: Article 16 of the Regulations of Fujian Province on Population and Family Planning30 states that in order to practice family planning, couples who already have children may choose to adopt safe, effective and appropriate contraceptive and birth control measures

propositions.text: On balance, the claimant could choose her own birth control method.
propositions.quote: I find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant could choose her own method of birth control.

propositions.text: The claimant says she lacks her family planning/IUD booklet, possibly exempting her from reporting to officials.
propositions.quote: the claimant maintains that she does not have her family planning/IUD booklet since it was taken by family planning officials and thus, she may not have to report to them at all.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds even if the Canadian-born child counts, the claimant could choose birth control and may not have to report to officials.

propositions.text: The claimants are not Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the Act.
propositions.quote: Based on the totality of the evidence in this particular case, I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees under s. 96 nor persons in need of protection under s. 97 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes the claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under the Act.

propositions.text: The Refugee Protection Division rejects the claimants' claims.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims.

paragraphs.summary: The Refugee Protection Division rejects the claimants' claims.
